content: Malignant wounds are a severe and distressing complication of cancer, typically occurring in the final six months of life. These wounds most commonly develop in areas such as the breast, chest wall, or head and neck. They are notoriously difficult to manage effectively and are associated with symptoms such as pain, excessive wound exudate, foul odour, and a significant risk of haemorrhage. For patients with advanced cancer, these symptoms can be profoundly distressing. The primary goal of treatment for malignant wounds is palliative, focusing on alleviating pain, controlling infection and odour, managing exudate, and protecting the surrounding skin from further damage. Malignant wounds are characterized by tissue degradation and necrosis, which create an environment conducive to the proliferation of both anaerobic and aerobic bacteria. The use of systemic antibiotics in this context aims to eliminate these bacteria, reduce associated symptoms such as odour, and potentially promote wound healing. To evaluate the effects of systemic antibiotics on malignant wounds, a systematic review was conducted. The search for relevant studies was comprehensive, encompassing multiple electronic databases, clinical trial registries, grey literature, and dissertation repositories. The search was completed in March 2017. The inclusion criteria were limited to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed the effects of systemic antibiotics on malignant wounds. Only one study met the inclusion criteria for this review. This study was a prospective, double-blind, cross-over trial that compared the effects of systemic metronidazole with a placebo on malodour in malignant wounds. Nine participants with fungating wounds and significant odour were recruited, and six of them completed both the intervention (metronidazole) and control (placebo) phases of the trial. Each phase lasted 14 days, separated by a 14-day washout period. The study reported on two primary outcomes: malodour and adverse effects of treatment. The mean malodour score for the metronidazole group was 1.17 (standard deviation [SD] 1.60), while the mean score for the placebo group was 3.33 (SD 0.82). The mean difference (MD) between the groups was -2.16 (95% confidence interval [CI] -3.6 to -0.72). However, the quality of evidence for this outcome was rated as very low due to a high risk of attrition bias (33% loss to follow-up) and serious imprecision caused by the small sample size. No adverse effects were reported in either the metronidazole or placebo groups. The authors concluded that it remains uncertain whether systemic metronidazole reduces malodour in patients with malignant wounds. This uncertainty is due to the inclusion of only a single study with a high risk of bias and a very small sample size, which focused exclusively on patients with breast cancer. Further research is necessary to confirm these findings and to explore the effects of systemic metronidazole and other antibiotics on additional outcomes, such as quality of life, pain relief, exudate management, and tumour containment in patients with malignant wounds.
